factor-gcf.why: Factoring turns a sum into a product, and a product is what lets you solve equations — because a product can only be zero when one of its parts is. Pulling out the greatest common factor is always the first move: it makes everything that follows smaller.
traps: Take out the *greatest* common factor, including any shared power of the variable, or you will be factoring again a minute later.
Expand your answer back as a check. It costs ten seconds and catches a dropped term.

factor-trinomial-1.why: For ~x^{2} + bx + c~ you need two numbers that multiply to ~c~ and add to ~b~. That works because expanding ~(x+p)(x+q)~ gives exactly ~x^{2} + (p+q)x + pq~ — you are reading the expansion backwards.
traps: Signs follow a pattern: ~c~ positive means both numbers share the sign of ~b~; ~c~ negative means they have opposite signs. Using it narrows the search immediately.

factor-trinomial-a.why: With a leading coefficient the search is wider, so use structure instead of guessing: multiply ~a~ by ~c~, find two numbers multiplying to that and adding to ~b~, split the middle term, then factor by grouping. It is mechanical and it always works.
traps: Take out any common factor before starting. Factoring ~6x^{2} + 15x + 6~ without first removing the 3 makes the AC search three times harder.

factor-difference-squares.why: ~a^{2} - b^{2} = (a+b)(a-b)~ is worth recognising on sight, because the middle terms cancel. It turns up constantly in simplifying fractions, rationalising denominators and mental arithmetic (~99 \times 101 = 100^{2} - 1~).
traps: A *sum* of squares does not factor over the integers. ~x^{2} + 9~ is already finished.
Check for a repeat: ~x^{4} - 16~ factors to ~(x^{2}+4)(x^{2}-4)~, and the second bracket factors again.

factor-grouping.why: With four terms, pair them up, factor each pair, and hope the same bracket appears in both — then take it out. This is also the engine inside the AC method for hard trinomials, so it is worth being comfortable with.
traps: If the two brackets do not match, try a different pairing before concluding it will not factor.
Watch the sign when the third term is negative: factor out ~-1~ with it if that makes the brackets agree.

factor-strategy.why: Factoring is a decision, not a single procedure. Always pull out the common factor first, then count terms: two suggests a difference of squares, three a trinomial, four grouping. Having that order in mind beats trying things at random.
traps: Many expressions need two steps. After one successful factoring, look at each bracket and ask whether it factors again.
